title: ChatGPT as Information Intermediary: Media Partnerships, Sycophancy, and the Pricing of Earnings News
abstract: Generative AI has become an increasingly important channel through which investors acquire financial news, yet little is known about how its content selection and framing affect capital markets. We study ChatGPT's role as an information intermediary around earnings announcements using two sources of variation: the staggered rollout of OpenAI's content-licensing partnerships with major news organizations and the April 2025 GPT-4o sycophancy episode. We first show that OpenAI's content partnerships sharply increase AI-referred traffic to partner outlets without a comparable increase in overall website traffic. Turning to market outcomes, greater partner coverage is associated with a stronger immediate response to favorable earnings surprises, followed by weaker subsequent returns for the strongest good news, and with more negative sixty-day returns for the most unfavorable earnings surprises. Consistent with an AI-mediated channel, these pricing patterns are more pronounced when the covering partner outlets have greater AI-referral intensity. Greater partner coverage is also associated with higher abnormal Google search activity, suggesting that the partnerships increase the salience of earnings news. To provide stronger causal evidence on the framing mechanism, we exploit the temporary GPT-4o sycophancy episode. During the episode, each additional partner article is associated with bad-news announcement returns approximately 0.35 percentage points less negative, indicating that more agreeable AI framing attenuated the market's immediate response to unfavorable news. Finally, we use a prompt-based experiment and find that each additional partner outlet increases the probability that GPT-4o identifies a firm's earnings announcement as notable by 3.2 percentage points, controlling for overall media coverage. Together, the findings show that AI content partnerships create a selective and distorting information channel with measurable consequences for price discovery and investor attention.
why: LLM as real market intermediary; natural experiments; pricing data; updates priors on efficiency.

title: The Great Codification: GenAI and Intangible Capital
abstract: Does artificial intelligence raise or destroy the value of intangible capital? We show that the answer depends on where that capital is stored. We construct the first task-based measure of the composition of the intangible capital embedded in firms' workforces, classifying all 19,265 U.S. work tasks by the type of intangible capital they produce or deploy, the codifiability of their method, the locus of the underlying knowledge, and their exposure to chatbots and agentic AI. Intangible-intensive firms gained value at the release of ChatGPT but lost value when new agentic AI capabilities were incorporated into stock prices in early 2026. We use a model with two storage media for intangible capital to explain the reversal: chatbots raise the value of human-stored knowledge, while agents make it economically and technologically feasible for codifiable knowledge to move into firm-owned software--creating value for the firm where the codified artifact is firm-specific and destroying it where it is portable and can be copied across firms. Consistent with the model, the market payoff to codifiability at the agentic capability event rises steeply with firm-specificity, and employment declines concentrate in codifiable occupations.
why: 19k U.S. tasks; stock price evaluation; surprising ChatGPT+ agents− reversal.

title: Regulatory Semantic Drift: When Preference-based Correction Fails Silently, FINCAC40, a Sixteen-year AMF Corpus (2010-2026) for Evaluating the Temporal Robustness of LLMs in ESG Classification
abstract: Does an LLM trained on the standardized vocabulary of the CSRD (2023) recognize a sustainability issue formulated a decade earlier in a different register? This question of temporal robustness had remained untested for French documents, for lack of a multi-regime corpus sampled without bias toward recent documents. For this first version, we present FINCAC40: 313,898 paragraphs from 23,144 AMF documents (CAC 40, 2010-2026), a Gold Standard of 140 ESRS-annotated paragraphs, and a stratified sampling protocol that avoids this bias. Across four LLMs, the result is heterogeneous: GPT-4o and Mistral-Large miss two out of three CSRD documents before 2015 but almost none after (∆F N R = +0.54 and +0.45), Mistral-7B exhibits the opposite trend, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 under-classifies almost everything, whatever the era. A linear probe of Mistral-7B confirms an above-chance temporal encoding (45.0% vs 30.7%), distributed over most layers. These results document an association between regulatory era and error rate for some of the models. Finally, we document the failure, over two iterations, of a correction by preference optimization (ORPO): total collapse in the first run, then collapse onto a refuge category in the second (precision 5.3% on ESRS2, FPR 64.9%, failures degrading from 0 to 30.7%). In both cases, nothing in the training metrics (loss, accuracy) made it possible to detect the collapse: only a downstream, task-specific evaluation reveals it. Correcting one bias through preference optimization can thus create another, more severe one, with no training signal to indicate it. It is therefore a concrete case of shortcut learning under a constrained data regime. Corpus, annotations, code and artifacts, including those of the failure, are released in open access at https://github.com/cdieng0/fincac.
why: Evaluation work on temporal robustness; FINCAC40 dataset, real financial documents, reveals brittleness.

title: Unknown Is Not Zero: Heat Stress, Data-Center Power-Demand Exposure, and Utility Volatility
abstract: This paper asks whether service-territory heat stress and disclosed data-center power-demand exposure jointly amplify the volatility of U.S. listed electric utilities. Its principal finding is methodological but empirically consequential: pre-disclosure silence is not a verified zero. The study constructs an auditable point-in-time chain from dated operating or binding customer-load megawatts to the regulated utility, the applicable EIA Form 861 peak-load denominator, a representative NOAA station, daily parent-company returns, and lag-available financial controls. Ten issuers satisfy a broad data-center four-quarter evidence rule over 2021-2025, although the measure is not uniformly AI-specific and one issuer is predominantly exposed to cryptocurrency hosting. Reclassifying 8,685 legacy zerocoded issuer-days as unknown leaves 3,855 positive-disclosure issuer-days and 212 complete portfolio observations across nine variance-recursion segments. The measurement path is non-monotone: the uncentered interaction is 0.143 in the legacy zero-coded panel and 0.060 when OTTR is excluded; after the common-positive restriction it reaches-2.000 at the coefficient bound, while centering yields an interior estimate of-0.118. Before centering, Corr(C,C×A)=0.979 and the interaction VIF is 29.4; centering lowers the VIF to 1.09. In the final Student-t GARCH-X specification, AIC and BIC select the no-interaction model and a 499-replication conditional parametric bootstrap does not reject it (LR=1.638, p=0.324). The current design therefore fails to detect heat-by-load amplification; it does not establish that the population effect is zero. H3 remains untested, and the pre-specified Markov-switching extension is not estimated. Positively, the audit identifies how exposure coding and coordinate construction can manufacture apparent interaction evidence, supplies a reusable regulatory-data architecture, and defines an advance rule under which a longer panel can retest the same hypotheses without redefining the original evidence.
why: Novel methodological finding: pre-disclosure silence is not zero; real data, auditable chain.

title: Signal Correlation, IC, and PnL Dependence
abstract: Signal correlation and PnL correlation are correlations over different index sets - across assets at each date versus across dates for scalar payoffs - and practitioners often treat the first as a proxy for the second. We give an exact decomposition that shows what that proxy sees and what it discards. We recall that at each date a normalized signal's projection onto the realized demeaned return direction is its realized cross-sectional Pearson IC, so that fixed-signal PnL is return dispersion times IC (Qian and Hua, 2004), and we identify the normalized similarity of two signals in the orthogonal complement as their partial correlation controlling for realized returns; the residual rotational freedom is an orthogonal gauge whose invariants are the transverse Gram matrix. Signal correlation therefore equals an uncentered IC cross-moment plus transverse similarity, while Pearson PnL correlation centers and dispersion-weights the IC series alone. Our main result is a non-identifiability theorem: absent constraints on transverse geometry, neither correlation bounds or orders the other, which sharpens the simulation finding of Sorensen, Qian, Schoen, and Hua (2004) into an exact statement. For normalized ensembles the transverse Gram matrix re-enters through the normalization denominator; the ex post optimal combination under Euclidean and general covariance-risk metrics is the classical multiple-correlation bound, and we show that the two rules agree for every longitudinal exposure if and only if the risk metric is isotropic on the signal span. The classical exact null law of partial correlation under isotropy, a synthetic mechanism illustration at weak-IC scales, and inference guidance under temporal dependence complete the treatment.
why: Foundational quant insight: exact IC/PnL decomposition clarifies signal correlation limits.

title: Adversarial Training for Tabular Credit Scoring: A Multi-Attack Robustness Evaluation in P2P Lending
abstract: Machine learning-based credit scoring is increasingly central to Peer-to-Peer (P2P) lending, yet its resilience to adversarial manipulation, where applicants strategically alter self-reported inputs to secure favourable decisions, remains poorly understood. Most adversarial-robustness evidence comes from image and text domains and evaluates a single attack against a matching defence, offering little guidance on how defences generalise across attack types in tabular credit data. We address this with a systematic train-test robustness benchmark on a large Lending Club subset, spanning three model families (logistic regression, a feed-forward neural network, and a transformer for tabular data) and four attacks confined to applicant-mutable features: Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM), Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), Salt-and-Pepper (S&P) noise, and DeepFool, plus a mixed-attack regime. Across a full grid evaluated with stratified cross-validation, adversarial training sharply improves robustness against the attack it is trained on and transfers well within the gradient-based family, but transfers weakly to non-gradient corruption, so single-attack defences overstate real-world resilience. Mixed training delivers the most balanced robustness across heterogeneous attacks while preserving clean-test performance, supporting multi-attack stress testing in credit-model governance.
why: Real credit risk (adversarial applicant manipulation); Lending Club data; systematic robustness.

title: dexamine: A Python package for Uniswap event data on Ethereum
abstract: Decentralized exchanges record trading and liquidity provision on public blockchains, but empirical analysis requires interpreting these records and linking them to execution metadata. dexamine is a Python package that parses Uniswap v2 and v3 events on Ethereum. It converts transaction receipt logs into observations of trades and liquidity changes, with token quantities, pool state, transaction order, and gas information. The package separates data retrieval, contract metadata, protocol interpretation, and output construction. The repository provides recorded Ethereum responses and an offline reproducible example, and version 1 has been used to construct data for an empirical study of price discovery in decentralized markets.
why: Released code and data for Uniswap microstructure; reproducible; immediately usable.

title: Cyber-Financial Contagion: Modeling the Propagation of an AI Vendor Compromise Through the Banking System
abstract: The banking system now depends on a small set of shared artificial intelligence vendors for fraud screening, credit decisioning, anti-money-laundering triage, customer analytics, and internal decision support. This paper studies how a compromise inside one of those vendors can propagate along a chain of operational, informational, and financial linkages until it triggers losses that look, from the outside, like a classical banking crisis. We build a four-layer heterogeneous network that couples AI vendors, financial institutions, interbank exposures, and customer accounts, and we propose CFC-Prop, a stochastic epidemic-and-clearing model that runs on that network. On a synthetic dataset with 60 vendors, 220 banks, roughly 2,500 vendor-bank service edges, and 1,400 interbank exposures, CFC-Prop reproduces the heavy-tailed loss distributions and the sharp dependence on patch latency that are consistent with prior cyber-financial evidence. We also train an early-warning model, CFC-GNN, that uses vendor-side incident telemetry and graph structure to flag high-cascade-risk vendors before impact. Across four baselines the proposed model reaches AUROC 0.82 and AUPRC 0.60 while keeping calibration errors bounded. We release the full code, synthetic data, and reproducible scripts. The results argue that cyber concentration among AI vendors is a first-order financial-stability problem and give supervisors a concrete quantitative tool for reasoning about it.
why: Novel vendor contagion network model; synthetic data only; framework stage.

title: The Log S-fBM model: Statistical analysis
abstract: The Log S-fBM model, introduced by Wu et al., is a stochastic volatility model whose log volatility is a stationary fractional Brownian motion (S-fBM): a stationary Gaussian process with power-decaying autocovariance driven by the Hurst exponent $H$, and variance scaled by an intermittency coefficient. A key property is that it reconciles rough volatility, where $H$ is typically near $0.1$ (see Gatheral et al.), with multifractal volatility, where $H$ is close to $0$ as in Bacry, Muzy et al.: the model's volatility measure converges to a multifractal random measure as $H\to0$. Numerical findings in Wu et al. show intermittency of order $0.02$ across financial assets, motivating a small intermittency approximation of log volatility moments for calibration via the general method of moments (GMM). In this work, we conduct a statistical analysis of the Log S-fBM model. We derive scaling properties of the S-fBM process and the Log S-fBM integrated volatility measure, present deviation inequalities with tail distributions sensitive to $H$ and intermittency, and develop a hypothesis test for the null Hurst exponent, i.e.\ rough versus multifractal dynamics. Finally, we revisit scale invariance of the log volatility increment process via explicit small-intermittency formulas, reproducing analogous properties in both regimes.
why: Solid rough volatility theory; no data or calibration results shown.

title: The Era by Eon Benchmark: A Generated Enterprise Estate with Exact Ground Truth for Benchmarking LLM Agents
abstract: LLM agents for enterprise systems of record cannot be evaluated on customer production data, and no existing substitute provides ground truth. We present the Era by Eon Benchmark for evaluating LLM agents that use enterprise tools. The benchmark is built around a complete fictional company. It includes product simulators, company-specific internal databases, benchmark questions, and computed answer keys. Industry, company size, business model, application portfolio, and a seed define each company. One seeded entity graph supplies shared company data to simulators of Salesforce, Zendesk, Slack, Gong, and other products. A questionconditioned generator creates the schemas and records for internal databases. It takes shared entities, keys, and values from the same graph before generating database-specific facts. Both mechanisms therefore describe one consistent enterprise estate. Every expected answer is computed from the final records, so grading is exact. Design and answer-key checks validate the internal databases. A realism scorecard and adversarial detector validate the entity graph. Across 23 generated companies, the mean realism score rose from 61.8 to 97.0, with zero records flagged as synthetic. In the reported simulator-track comparison, nine models answered the same 33 questions three times each. Accuracy estimates ranged from 42.4% to 76.8%, and three of 36 pairwise differences remained supported after correction.
why: Useful LLM agent benchmark; not finance-specific, infrastructure-focused.

title: Comparative Analysis of CKKS and BGV Homomorphic Schemes for Federated Credit Scoring
abstract: The adoption of Federated Learning (FL) for credit scoring presents a critical challenge: enabling collaborative model training across financial institutions while preserving the strict confidentiality of sensitive customer financial data. Homomorphic Encryption (HE) has emerged as a pivotal privacy-preserving technology for this domain, allowing computations on encrypted data. However, selecting the optimal HE scheme is non-trivial, as it requires navigating a complex trade-off between computational efficiency, communication overhead, and the specific requirements of the machine learning operations involved. This paper presents a comparative analysis of two leading HE schemes-the Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song (CKKS) scheme, which supports approximate floating-point arithmetic, and the Brakerski-Gentry-Vaikuntanathan (BGV) scheme, which excels in exact integer arithmetic-within the context of federated credit scoring. We evaluate the performance of both schemes across key metrics, including encryption and decryption time, per-operation latency (especially for multiplication and rotation), ciphertext expansion, and communication costs during the federated aggregation process. Our analysis is grounded in the practical constraints of a logistic regression model, a standard algorithm in credit scoring, and considers the impact of varying parameter sets and security levels. The findings reveal that while CKKS offers superior computational speed and lower memory footprint for the core linear algebra operations due to its native approximate arithmetic, it introduces precision errors that can subtly affect model convergence and final scoring accuracy. Conversely, BGV provides deterministic, exact computations but at a significantly higher computational cost and ciphertext expansion, potentially becoming a bottleneck in a multi-party FL setting with numerous institutions. We conclude by providing a set of practical guidelines for selecting between CKKS and BGV based on institutional priorities, such as tolerances for accuracy loss, computational budgets, and network constraints, thereby offering a roadmap for the secure and efficient deployment of privacy-preserving credit scoring systems in the financial sector.
why: Cryptographic scheme comparison; no financial results shown.

title: Liquidity Risk Modeling: Assessing Systemic Funding Liquidity Shocks in Fixed-Income Portfolios During Macroeconomic Downturns
abstract: This paper investigates the systemic funding liquidity risk in fixed-income portfolios, particularly during periods of macroeconomic downturns. We develop a robust modeling framework to identify and quantify the impact of liquidity shocks across various fixed-income asset classes. Utilizing a combination of econometric techniques and machine learning algorithms, our approach aims to capture the non-linear dynamics and interconnectedness within financial markets. The findings provide critical insights for risk managers, policymakers, and institutional investors in developing more resilient portfolio strategies and enhancing financial stability. We demonstrate the utility of our model through case studies of historical downturns, highlighting key transmission channels and vulnerabilities. Our framework further contributes to the literature by bridging traditional macroeconomic stress testing with modern predictive analytics. Unlike conventional models that treat liquidity as exogenous, we endogenize funding liquidity as a dynamic variable driven by market sentiment, monetary policy shifts, and balance sheet constraints. By combining Vector Autoregression (VAR) for impulse response analysis with Random Forest classifiers for early warning signals, the model offers both explanatory power and practical forecasting capability. This dual approach allows institutions to not only understand how liquidity shocks propagate during downturns but also to anticipate and mitigate them before they materialize into systemic events.
why: Generic liquidity framework; case studies without novel contribution.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Portfolio Optimization in the Indian Equity Market: A Comparative Study of A2C, DDPG, PPO, SAC, and TD3
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for sequential decision-making in financial portfolio management, yet most published evaluations focus on U.S. or Chinese equity markets. This paper presents an end-to-end empirical study of five model-free deep RL algorithms: Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C), Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), and Twin Delayed DDPG (TD3), applied to dynamic asset allocation across 48 constituents of the NIFTY 50 index. Using the FinRL framework, we construct a custom trading environment with nine technical indicators (MACD, RSI, CCI, DX, Bollinger Bands, and moving averages) as state features, train each agent on a one-year historical window (Jan 2024-Jan 2025), and backtest on a subsequent 75-trading-day held-out window (Jan-Apr 2025) against a simulated $1,000,000 portfolio and the NIFTY 50 index benchmark. A2C achieved the highest return (+5.15%), followed by DDPG (+2.02%), while PPO, TD3, and SAC posted losses of-15.64%,-10.33%, and-20.05% respectively, a 25.2-percentage-point spread between best and worst agent. We report the full experimental pipeline, discuss confounding factors including an unequal training budget across algorithms, and outline limitations that should be addressed before any live deployment.
why: RL portfolio predictor; 75-day backtest is too short; no transaction costs mentioned.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Multi-Indicator Confluence Frameworks for Cryptocurrency Trading Signal Optimisation: Evidence from Major Digital Assets
abstract: This study develops an explainable artificial intelligence framework designed to optimise cryptocurrency trading signals by integrating established technical indicators with advanced ensemble machine learning techniques. Drawing on 29,738 daily observations spanning ten major global digital assets from 2016 to 2026, the framework combines momentum, volatility, and trend-confirmation indicators-including the Relative Strength Index, Bollinger Bands, Average True Range, and Simple Moving Average crossovers-with various ensemble models such as Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost. Principal Component Analysis and K-Means clustering are employed to reduce dimensional redundancy and segment assets into distinct risk-return profiles, while SHAP-based explainability methods ensure model transparency and regulatory accountability. Empirical results demonstrate that XGBoost delivers the strongest predictive accuracy, achieving an R² of 0.43 on out-of-sample data. Comprehensive backtesting reveals that the AI-enhanced confluence framework substantially outperforms passive buy-and-hold strategies, with a Sharpe ratio of 1.81 versus 0.81, a maximum drawdown reduced from 78% to 37%, and a win rate of 69%. SHAP analysis further identifies Bollinger %B, Relative Strength Index, and Average True Range as the most influential predictive features, with volatility indicators dominating bearish regimes and momentum indicators exerting greater influence during bullish market periods. By effectively filtering market noise through high-confidence, multidimensional signal-confirmation requirements, the proposed framework offers a robust, practical, scalable, and fully interpretable systematic approach to responsible algorithmic trading and digital asset portfolio management across diverse and evolving market conditions.
why: XGBoost on crypto; no transaction costs, baselines, or out-of-sample discipline.

title: Geometric and Arithmetic Likelihood Aggregation for Diffusions with Heterogeneous Volatility
abstract: We study how to combine diffusion models that disagree about drift and covariance. Candidate-first relative-entropy minimization gives geometric pooling, whereas expert-first minimization gives the arithmetic mixture associated with weighted logarithmic wealth. Different quadratic variations can make path-space entropy infinite, and the arithmetic mixture need not be a Markov diffusion. We therefore specify a local criterion combining drift information, normalized by the second argument's covariance, with quadratic transport between Gaussian shocks in a fixed state metric. A Gaussian identity and an Euler convergence estimate justify this chosen criterion. The expert-first projection has posterior-mean drift and an inverse-covariance penalty for drift dispersion; in one dimension this penalty increases volatility. For Ornstein--Uhlenbeck experts with a common mean-reversion rate, coefficient regularity holds on the full horizon for common volatility and away from the initial time for heterogeneous volatilities. The candidate-first problem has a Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman characterization. Its matrix covariance selector reduces by congruence to a Bures--Wasserstein barycenter. The condition $H+λM\succ0$, with value Hessian $H$ and state metric $M$, is sharp for finiteness of the unrestricted local covariance problem; compact constraints keep that problem finite. A covariance-disagreement budget interprets the penalty parameter. Linear--quadratic, exact-transition, and financial examples distinguish dynamic volatility reduction, drift-dispersion inflation, and martingale restrictions.
why: Pure theory on combining diffusions; no data or implementation.

title: Quantum Feature Engineering for Credit Default Prediction: When and Why IQP Circuits Help Linear Classifiers
abstract: Credit default prediction is a tabular classification problem in which modest gains in F1 translate directly into reduced financial exposure. We ask whether Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time (IQP) circuits can produce features that improve a classifier over both its raw classical baseline and Kernel PCA - the strongest unsupervised classical non-linear alternative - at an equal feature budget. The dataset provides 23 financial attributes per client; for an n-qubit circuit we select n of them, encode each as a rotation angle, and read 2n expectation values back out as new features. The motivation for using a quantum circuit is computational: an n-qubit IQP circuit runs in constant depth and encodes feature correlations in a 2^n-dimensional Hilbert space, whereas classical simulation of its exact output statistics scales exponentially in n. Using the UCI Default of Credit Card Clients dataset and five-fold cross-validation, we find that appending 16 IQP features (n = 8 qubits) to a Logistic Regression model raises F1 from 0.462 to 0.517 (+0.055, p < 0.0001). Kernel PCA, the next-best method, reaches only 0.493 at the same feature count; the gap survives Benjamini-Hochberg correction across 12 tests (p = 0.00007). No other classifier - Random Forest, SVM, XGBoost, or k-NN - benefits, which points to a linear-expressivity mechanism rather than a generic improvement. We also show that how the 8 input features are chosen matters: Random Forest importance-guided selection reaches F1 = 0.523, while encoding maximally uncorrelated features drops it to 0.496, demonstrating that the circuit amplifies informative structure rather than creating it from scratch.
why: Quantum circuits for credit scoring; not practically available; no performance evidence.

title: Beyond Model Governance: A Deployment Assurance Architecture for Consequential AI Systems in Financial Services
abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering the production processes of regulated financial institutions faster than the governance instruments designed to oversee it. Existing instruments are individually sophisticated: horizontal frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the European Union's AI Act organise risk management around systems and organisations, while financial-sector regimes, the Reserve Bank of India's FREE-AI framework and draft Model Risk Management guidance, the revised US interagency model-risk guidance (SR 26-2) and the UK PRA's SS1/23, provide deep disciplines for model validation, operational resilience and third-party risk. Yet these mechanisms remain distributed across governance domains and no instrument requires an institution, at a single decision point, to justify that AI and its chosen level of technological complexity, is necessary rather than a simpler sufficient alternative; to assemble multidimensional evidence into one deploymentboundary artefact; to articulate business, liability and strategic-information consequences; and to record explicit, conditioned institutional acceptance that is periodically reexamined. The gap is sharpened by SR 26-2, which expressly excludes generative and agentic AI from its scope. This paper proposes the AI Deployment Assurance Framework (AIDAF), a deployment-level assurance architecture that (i) operationalises technological necessity as an approval-contingent gate whose justificatory burden rises with technological complexity; (ii) integrates established risk-management, measurement and assurance mechanisms into a staged pipeline culminating in a Risk Articulation Report, a financial-sector adaptation of the assurance-case tradition; and (iii) requires evidence-based institutional risk acceptance with control-operation verifiability and periodic re-justification, including authority to retire or replace deployments with less complex solutions. The framework is developed through structured comparative analysis of major AI-governance and financial-sector instruments and illustrated with hypothetical scenarios. Limitations include its conceptual character and qualitative comparison method.
why: Governance position paper; no methods or implementation.

title: Beyond "Is It a Model?" A Capability-based Framework for Agentic AI Governance in Financial Institutions
abstract: Revised U.S. model risk management guidance issued in April 2026 excludes generative and agentic AI models from its scope while directing banking organizations to determine appropriate governance for systems the guidance does not cover. This paper argues that the resulting governance question should not be reduced to whether agentic AI belongs inside or outside Model Risk Management (MRM). More fundamentally, formal model determination is only one routing decision within a broader enterprise governance perimeter. For purposes of this paper, agentic AI refers to AI-enabled systems capable of pursuing objectives through multi-step planning or execution, dynamically selecting or invoking tools and external resources, and, where authorized, taking actions that alter an external system or process with varying degrees of human oversight. An AI-enabled workflow may fall outside the supervisory definition of a model and nevertheless materially select evidence for a regulated decision, access sensitive production data, invoke privileged tools, communicate with customers, or change external state. The paper therefore proposes a capability profile that precedes model determination and distinguishes baseline AI functionality from capabilities that require heightened cross-functional review. It then examines what effective challenge should establish when the risk arises from an end-to-end workflow rather than a single model component. The proposed approach is organized around three questions: does the system perform as intended; what does it materially influence; and what is it technically allowed to do? For materially consequential autonomous actions, traceability becomes a deployment prerequisite whose rigor should increase with delegated authority, consequence, and irreversibility. The contribution is deliberately narrow: a sequencing and assurance logic that connects AI classification, MRM scope, cross-functional control evidence, deployment conditions, and re-entry without treating every agent as a model or inventing a separate AI risk regime.
why: Agentic AI governance paper; rejected category (position paper).

title: Enhancing Financial Accuracy and Reliability: A Study on AI-Driven Accounting Automation
abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into accounting practices has emerged as a transformative force in enhancing financial accuracy, operational efficiency, and decision-making processes. This study investigates the impact of AI-driven accounting automation on the accuracy and reliability of financial reporting within contemporary business environments. For the study, primary data were collected from accountants, accounts managers, finance analysts, and academic researchers. To assess whether perceptions significantly differed from a neutral stance, a one-sample t-test was applied, using a test value of , which represented the midpoint of the-point Likert scale. The research examines how accounting applications utilizing using AI-driven automation tools streamline routine tasks, including data entry, transaction categorization, reconciliation, and compliance monitoring. The results provide strong evidence that accounting professionals and academician perceive AI tools as significantly accurate and reliable in the context of accounting. The widespread agreement across various aspects of AI performance indicates a high level of trust and acceptance of these technologies. Such perceptions are essential for the continued integration of AI in professional practice, as positive user attitudes often drive adoption and effective utilization.
why: Survey via Likert scales; no empirical test or implementation.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Internal-Audit Efficiency and Accounting Information-System Cybersecurity: A Critical Synthesis and Research Agenda for the UAE
abstract: Purpose-This paper critically examines how artificial intelligence (AI) may reconfigure internal-audit efficiency and the security, integrity and resilience of accounting information systems (AIS), with particular attention to the United Arab Emirates (UAE). It asks when AI extends assurance capacity and when it redistributes, obscures or intensifies technological and accountability risks. Design/methodology/approach-The paper develops an integrative critical review spanning auditing, accounting information systems, information security, algorithmic governance and organizational theory. It synthesizes more than 60 peer-reviewed studies, including over 50 studies in internationally leading and predominantly Q1-ranked outlets, alongside authoritative UAE policy and professional frameworks. Published qualitative field studies are coded into themes concerning visibility, expertise, jurisdiction, explainability and control. A multi-level socio-technical model and a sequential, longitudinal mixedmethod research design are proposed for empirical testing in the UAE. Findings-AI can reduce routine effort, increase population coverage and accelerate anomaly detection, but efficiency is contingent on task-technology fit, data lineage, model validation, integration and auditor competence. Cybersecurity effects are ambivalent: AI improves surveillance while enlarging attack surfaces and creating model, privacy, third-party and automation risks. Published qualitative evidence shows that analytics can shift-not eliminate-professional judgement, produce new expert dependencies and transform audit evidence into contestable algorithmic outputs. Research limitations/implications-This is a critical synthesis and research-design paper rather than a report of original UAE fieldwork. Journal quartiles vary by database and year; outlet rankings should therefore be rechecked at submission. The proposed design offers a credible route to causal, processual and institutional evidence. Practical implications-UAE boards, regulators and chief audit executives should evaluate AI by assurance quality and residual risk rather than labour savings alone, establish independent model assurance, preserve human challenge and build auditable data and model lineages. Originality/value-The paper joins audit-automation and cybersecurity literatures that are usually treated separately and theorizes AI as an assurance-exposure duality. It develops a context-sensitive agenda for a highly digitalized, institutionally distinctive emerging economy.
why: Literature review synthesizing 60+ studies; no original contribution.

title: Fin Tech Innovation and Sustainable Supply Chains: Leveraging Digital Finance Innovation for ESG-Based Procurement, Supplier Risk Assessment, and Environmental Performance Monitoring
abstract: The convergence of financial technology (Fin Tech) and sustainable supply chain management (SSCM) has revamped the operational and strategic frameworks for global trade. Fin Tech advancements are rapidly becoming a major factor in assisting companies in meeting environmental, social, and governance (ESG) requirements, which are essential for fostering sustainable growth. The ways that digital finance tools-like block chain, AI, big data analytics, and digital payment platforms-assist in supplier risk assessment, environmental performance tracking, and ESG-based procurement are examined in this article. Drawing on recent empirical and theoretical literature, this study uses a qualitative approach and secondary data to investigate Fin Tech's revolutionary role in SSCM. Key findings indicate that digital finance technologies improve environmental monitoring by enabling supply chain traceability and transparency, speed up procurement processes through real-time ESG compliance checks, and enhance supplier risk management through predictive analytics.The paper contributes to the growing body of research on sustainability and digital transformation by providing a methodical analysis of Fin Tech capabilities. Policy implications emphasize the need for regulatory support, cross-sector collaboration, and capacity building to fully fulfill Fin Tech's promise in sustainable supply chains. The results provide credence to a digital-first approach to sustainability that places an emphasis on accountability, performance, and resilience.
why: Qualitative review of FinTech and ESG supply chains; no original data.

title: Generative Calculus II: Capability Attribution Under Augmentation Whole-Envelope Interaction Accounting for Resources, Information, Interfaces, and Rules
abstract: Modern AI capability is increasingly a property of an augmented system rather than a frozen model: test-time computation, retrieved evidence, tools, memory, interfaces, and control rules can all change what is feasible. Generative Calculus II (GC-II) asks where such gains come from. It lifts factorial attribution from scalar scores to task–scale–error–budget capability envelopes and defines an Envelope Attribution Spectrum using Boolean-lattice Möbius inversion. We prove exact attribution, additive-accounting characterization, endpoint non-identifiability, factorial identifiability, and strict refinement of scalar accuracy. We then prove a matched-summary whole-envelope separation: for every fixed projection order, there are balanced envelope families with identical low-order coordinate projections but exact membership-circuit complexities O(n) and Ω(2ⁿ/n), using classical Shannon circuit counting as the lower-bound ingredient. The accompanying public implementation provides reproducible computational results. On handwritten digits, third-order hold-out prediction reduces full-system error from 0.0795 to 0.0162. In a fixed-weight 16-condition FLAN-T5-small pilot comprising 240 evaluations, accuracy rises from 0.20 to 0.60, higher-order interaction mass is 0.4667, and third-order terms predict the held-out full system to machine precision. GC-II therefore separates model capability from system capability while making both attribution and reconstruction complexity auditable.
why: Pure theory, off-topic. No financial application.

title: On the Inability of Language Models to Stub Their Toe: Referential Collapse, Semantic Inflation, and the Disconnect Between Linguistic Competence and Grounded Understanding
abstract: This paper examines a structural mismatch between the linguistic conventions rewarded in academic writing and the referential function language originally evolved to serve. We demonstrate this mismatch using a single physical object as a grounding example throughout, showing how verbosity is systematically rewarded while referential clarity is penalized in the corpora that constitute the training data for large language models. We trace the philosophical foundations of this problem through Plato's concerns about writing, Harnad's symbol grounding problem, and contemporary research on embodied cognition. We argue that language models inherit an inverted training signal that optimizes for elaboration rather than reference, producing systems that can describe objects indenitely but cannot interact with them. The analysis concludes that understanding occurs exclusively in the human reader, not in the system producing text, with implications for how we deploy these systems in educational and decision-making contexts.
why: Off-topic; philosophical LLM critique with no finance relevance.

title: Adaptive Entangled Game Modules in Artificial General Intelligence
abstract: We introduce a probability-wave framework for modeling the collective behavior of interacting adaptive agents, deriving testable eigenmodes through a generalized behavioral intelligence (GBI) nonlocal probability-wave equation. This framework captures a broad range of human intelligence behaviors with analytical mechanisms and offers an indirect method to examine the Liu-Chen-Ao (LCA) hypothesis of nonlocal entangled nerve fibers in the brain through collective trader behaviors. Our empirical analysis of Chinese intraday stock market data demonstrates that adaptive entangled game modes explain 82-94% (89% overall) of observed decision patterns, a sharp contrast to the predictions of neoclassical finance based on independent rational agents. Moreover, 2-12% of behaviors show adaption to intraday news, events, and environments, characterized by dual equilibrium states and abrupt reference point shifts, while purely independent modes occur in less than 5% of cases. These findings empirically support the LCA hypothesis, as observable trading behaviors reflect underlying brain mechanisms and internal intelligence decision-making in behavioral psychology. Our results highlight the necessity of incorporating adaptive entangled game modules into artificial general intelligence (AGI) architectures, addressing the limitations of conventional artificial neural network (ANN)-based AI, which relies on trillions of opaque parameters. By integrating ANN-based AI with probability-wave-based entangled-brain simulations, machine learning can enrich AGI foundation models (FMs) and facilitate the development of human-like processing units (HPUs) that leverage brain-inspired mechanisms. Such HPUs may ultimately create more compact, efficient, and robust AGI systems, particularly for embodied intelligence and robotics.

title: PACE: Perceived-Latency-Aware Cascading Service Routing and Filler Control for QoE-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Dialogue Serving
abstract: We present the PACE, a framework for retrieval-augmented dialogue serving that formalizes Perceived Time-to-First-Response (PTFR) as a QoE objective and minimizes it under quality/cost constraints. Unlike prior work on cascaded routing, semantic caching, or adaptive retrieval, PACE jointly controls which answer source composes the response and what fills the waiting window. Deployed on a humanoid-robot sales service, it combines three mechanisms: a load-adaptive cascading router, a joint path-filler controller, and volatility-aware cache admission. On 75k CarQA requests, the cascade halves pure-LLM PTFR at P95 (0.29 vs 0.53s at c16). The adaptive controller reaches 0.41s P95, outperforming RAG by 2.4 times at high load with equal quality. The filler controller cuts calls by 94% with zero conflict. Volatility-aware admission reduces stale answers from 86% to 0%. A gating rule ensures the controller never worse than the baseline, with exposure bounded by one hold period. This is the first quantification of filler-answer conflict risk in deployed services.
why: Chatbot QoE optimization. Consumer retail, not finance.

title: In Medical Claims Data, Enhancing Predictive Performance for Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events Using Cross Attention
abstract: Medical claims data comprise the financial details, including the expenses and billing information, as well as the clinical information, such as the diagnoses and treatments, of patients visiting medical facilities. Recently, it has been acknowledged that large databases can be constructed from medical claims data for medical research purposes. However, the clinical information within these datasets is often medically unstructured, limiting its application in comprehensive analyses. This study enhances predictive model performance for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), a leading cause of death worldwide. Models that predict MACE are crucial to clinical practice guidelines. We utilize a cross-attention mechanism to develop a method that effectively weights the relationships between diagnoses and treatments. Effectively repre- senting the clinical information contained in medical claims data, this approach generates more representative features for predicting MACE. The ROC-AUC score of our proposed cross-attention-based model was 0.7720, higher than other benchmark models including the conventional atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease model, the light gradient boosting machine, and a self-attention-based model. These results indicate that integrating the clinical structure of medical claims data using a cross-attention mechanism significantly enhances the performance of predictive models.
why: Off-topic medical claims prediction; healthcare, not finance.
